Attention head redundancy in vision-language models (VLMs) is not a uniform property: heads that appear functionally redundant by standard importance metrics (gradient-norm attribution, Taylor expansion) during unimodal evaluation often become load-bearing during cross-modal alignment tasks, where they serve as soft routing mechanisms bridging visual token distributions to linguistic query spaces. The central question is whether pruning decisions made on task-specific fine-tuned VLMs are systematically biased toward removing heads that have undergone specialization drift — meaning heads that originally handled syntactic or positional functions in the language tower have been repurposed during visual instruction tuning to handle cross-modal grounding — causing them to register as "incoherent" by classical redundancy measures despite being functionally critical. The key concepts are: (1) pruning sensitivity asymmetry, the observation that sensitivity scores are not symmetric across modal origins of a head's learned function; (2) head specialization drift, where fine-tuning shifts a head's dominant eigenvector in attention weight space away from its pretraining attractor; and (3) cross-modal alignment pressure, the gradient signal that induces this drift by forcing language-tower heads to attend over visual token sequences they were never pretrained on. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is that standard one-shot or iterative magnitude pruning applied post-alignment fine-tuning will disproportionately remove drifted heads because their weight norms and gradient signals look diffuse — they're attending over high-dimensional, low-coherence visual patches — while heads doing clean, redundant linguistic work survive because they produce crisp, low-entropy attention patterns that score well on importance metrics, even though those heads are the expendable ones.

A drifted head exhibits elevated but structured entropy — not the flat, near-uniform attention distribution of a genuinely redundant head, but a modestly high-entropy pattern that retains weak spatial coherence across visual token grids, often clustering softly around salient patch regions without the sharp argmax peaks characteristic of linguistic heads attending to syntactic anchors. In LLaVA-style architectures, where a frozen or lightly-tuned language model receives projected visual tokens prepended to the sequence, drifted heads tend to develop what you might call diffuse grounding signatures: their attention mass spreads across 30–80 visual tokens rather than concentrating, because no single patch is "correct" in the way a syntactic head has a correct head-word to attend to — the head is performing aggregate scene representation, not token selection. Michel et al. (2019) and the subsequent Voita et al. (2019) work on linguistically-interpretable heads both calibrate importance under the assumption that low-entropy, high-confidence heads are doing real work; a head with entropy in the 3.5–4.5 nats range (on a 256-token visual prefix) will score near zero on their confidence-weighted importance metrics regardless of its actual contribution to the cross-modal alignment objective. Gradient-based estimators (Taylor first-order, as in Molchanov et al. 2017) compound this invisibility: the gradient signal through a drifted head is diffuse because its contribution to the loss is distributed — it influences the residual stream softly across many positions rather than decisively at a few, so the product of weight magnitude and gradient magnitude stays low even when ablating the head collapses cross-modal retrieval accuracy by several points. The cruel irony is that this diffuse-but-structured entropy profile is precisely what you'd expect from a head doing useful soft attention over a high-dimensional unstructured input, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from a head that has simply learned to approximate a flat prior while memorizing nothing — the distinguishing signal lives not in the entropy scalar but in the spatial covariance structure of the attention pattern across image regions, which standard scalar importance metrics never examine.
